clue.text: Gets on to bosses' groups

blocks.note: first meaning: climbs aboard, as onto a ship, bus or plane
second meaning: committees of directors who run companies

explanation.surface: Someone ingratiating themselves with management committees at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets on to' looks like 'makes contact with' the bosses; in fact it is one meaning alone, the verb for stepping aboard a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for embarking on a vehicle and the plural noun for directors' committees governing a company.

clue.text: The bear is shot — it will do this no more

definitions.text: it will do this no more
definitions.note: a cryptic pointer to a verb: what the dead bear can no longer do

indicators.note: something shot is wrecked or ruined, so the letters lose their original order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A hunter's bear has been shot dead and will never do this again.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the surface: 'it' is the bear, and what a shot bear will do no more is draw air. 'Shot' does double work as both the killing and the shuffle signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead animal no longer takes air into its lungs, so the activity it has stopped is respiration.

clue.text: Leading character getting top grade

blocks.note: first meaning: the first letter of the Greek alphabet
second meaning: the highest mark given to an essay or exam

explanation.surface: The star of a show being awarded the highest mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading character' suggests the hero of a play, but here the character is a letter, the one leading the Greek alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: It names the first Greek letter and, in British marking, the highest grade a piece of work can receive.

clue.text: Journalist turning up with drink for critical game?

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means flipping so the word reads from the bottom upward

blocks.note: ED is the usual short form of editor
an alcoholic drink made from apples

explanation.surface: A reporter arriving with a drink before a big match.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'turning up' means reading from the bottom upward, so the editor is written backwards above the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A deciding game settles the result of a tied contest, so it is the match on which everything depends.

clue.text: Admiral? Be nice initially and gesture respect

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
its opening letter
to bend the head or body as a mark of respect

explanation.surface: Advice on how to greet an admiral: be polite at first and bow.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is an example: the answer is one particular admiral, not the word for the rank.
explanation.definitionFit: John Benbow was a famous English naval commander of the late seventeenth century, an example of the rank named.

clue.text: Orders English dictionary — first requirement for solver

indicators.note: the first thing a word requires is its opening letter, so only that letter is kept

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
standard abbreviation
its opening letter

explanation.surface: Someone ordering an English dictionary, the first thing a crossword solver needs.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes the dictionary sound like the solver's essential kit, but 'first requirement for solver' only supplies one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Edicts are official decrees or commands issued by an authority, so they are orders in the plural noun sense.

clue.text: Dwelling in Somerset city — a building with water facilities

indicators.note: a home located in a town is labelled with the place name first, so the pieces are placed in that order

blocks.note: the Roman spa city in the English county of Somerset
a home

explanation.surface: A home in the city of Bath, described as a building with plumbing.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath is a city in Somerset, south-west England, famous for its Roman baths, which makes the definition doubly apt.
explanation.definitionFit: A bathhouse is a public building containing baths for washing or bathing, so it is a structure housing water amenities.

clue.text: Sang in hostilities, having suffered injury?

blocks.note: armed conflict between nations
lost blood from a wound

explanation.surface: A wounded soldier singing on the battlefield.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that bleeding is only one way of suffering an injury, so the second piece is an example rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To warble is to sing with trills and quavers, like a songbird, so the past tense matches the verb given.

clue.text: Going in a circle at all times

blocks.note: first meaning: travelling the full circuit of a dial, as the hands do
second meaning: continuously, day and night without a break

explanation.surface: Something that keeps circling endlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: The first meaning is literal: a hand going all the way round a watch face; the second is the idiom for nonstop activity.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase literally describes a complete circuit of a dial and idiomatically means continuously, through every hour of day and night.

clue.text: Retain castle's feature

blocks.note: first meaning: continue to possess, not give up
second meaning: the strongest central tower of a medieval fortress

explanation.surface: Preserving a characteristic part of a historic castle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retain' is a verb and the second half a noun, so the one word does two grammatical jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a verb for holding on to something and the noun for the fortified inner tower of a medieval stronghold.

clue.text: Church singers show off their cross

indicators.note: something off is wrong or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A church choir proudly displaying the crucifix they carry in procession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show off' reads as one phrasal verb, but it splits: 'show' only links, and 'off' alone signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Choristers are members of a choir, especially boys or men singing in a cathedral or parish church.

clue.text: Money found on street or beach?

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing placed on another comes after it, so the pieces are ordered

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation used in addresses
the currency of South Africa

explanation.surface: Where might you pick up cash lying about: on the road or the sand?
explanation.walkthrough: The rand is South Africa's currency, a common crossword source of 'money'.
explanation.definitionFit: Strand is a literary word for the shore of a sea, lake or river, the land along the water's edge.

clue.text: Essential truth found in mad and unpleasant place

definitions.note: points to the idiom 'in a nutshell'; the answer itself is a noun

blocks.note: informal for crazy
any thoroughly miserable place

explanation.surface: A philosopher discovering that the core truth lies somewhere crazy and grim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found in' seems to link definition to wordplay, but it belongs to the definition: the essentials are given 'in a nutshell'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'in a nutshell' means stated briefly with only the core points, so the summary lives inside this container.

clue.text: Belittle Ted in gear that's unconventional

indicators.note: unconventional means not in the usual order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Mocking a man named Ted for wearing odd clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gear' looks like clothing worth mocking; it is just letters to be rearranged with Ted and 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: To denigrate someone is to criticise them unfairly and play down their worth, which is to make them seem small.

clue.text: Job wasn't apt in time to change

definitions.note: an adjective phrase: what the biblical Job was not

indicators.note: changing something alters its form, so the letters take a new arrangement

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A job that did not suit someone at the moment it needed to change.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital J disguises the biblical Job as an occupation; the patience of Job is proverbial, so what he was not is the opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Job endured every trial without complaint, so the trait he famously lacked was restlessness or intolerance of delay.

clue.text: One pound for some tobacco

blocks.note: first meaning: British slang for a pound sterling
second meaning: a lump of tobacco for chewing

explanation.surface: Paying a pound for a little tobacco.
explanation.walkthrough: A quid is everyday British slang for one pound sterling; the tobacco sense is a plug kept in the cheek and chewed.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both British slang for a pound coin's worth of money and a piece of chewing tobacco.

clue.text: One dad or two?

blocks.note: surface reading: a puzzle about how many fathers someone has
setter's reading: the word means one father, yet it is spelt as the short word for dad written twice

explanation.surface: Someone unsure how many fathers there are.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the answer is a single father in meaning but looks like two of the two-letter word for dad side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a familiar, slightly old-fashioned word children use for their father.

clue.text: Support a new source of energy — it's a gas

indicators.note: a source is where something begins, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: something that holds a thing up
taken as written
standard abbreviation
its opening letter

explanation.surface: Backing a new energy source and announcing that it's great fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's a gas' sounds like slang for 'it's a laugh', but 'gas' is literal and 'source of energy' only gives one letter, not a fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: Propane is a flammable hydrocarbon, a colourless fuel stored in cylinders for heating and cooking.

clue.text: Protection round the Queen once showing respect

indicators.note: to go round something is to surround it, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: guarding against attack
Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen's cipher; 'once' because she has died

explanation.surface: Royal guards around Queen Elizabeth showing her courtesy.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, for Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword shorthand for the Queen; 'once' marks that Elizabeth II is no longer reigning.
explanation.definitionFit: Deference is polite submission to and regard for another person's status, wishes or authority.

clue.text: Serious listener gets a cosy spot?

blocks.note: the organ of hearing
a snug, comfortable place, like a bird's home

explanation.surface: A solemn audience member is given a comfortable seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Listener' looks like a person in the audience, but it is the organ that listens, a common crossword trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnest describes someone sincere and intensely grave in manner, lacking frivolity, the adjective sense required here.

clue.text: Agreement to provide musical event

blocks.note: first meaning: harmony of purpose
second meaning: a public performance of music

explanation.surface: A contract signed to stage a music show.
explanation.walkthrough: The agreement sense survives mainly in the phrase 'in concert', meaning acting together.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun means both joint accord between parties and a live public performance by musicians.

clue.text: Nasty men are becoming nastier

indicators.note: something nasty has been treated roughly, so the letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Unpleasant men growing even more unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nasty' looks like a description of the men, but it is the rearrangement signal, echoed by the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Meaner is the comparative of mean in its sense of unkind or spiteful, so it matches the comparative given.

clue.text: Norma let loose in Canadian city

indicators.note: something loose is no longer held in place, so the letters can move freely

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman called Norma is set free in a city in Canada.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let loose' reads as one phrase, but 'let' is part of the letters to rearrange and only 'loose' signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Montreal is the largest city in the province of Quebec, an example of a Canadian city.

clue.text: Sailor's appraisal

blocks.note: first meaning: a non-commissioned sailor in the British navy
second meaning: an assessment or score

explanation.surface: A seaman's performance review.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe s looks possessive but stands for 'is'. In the Royal Navy, a rating is an ordinary sailor rather than an officer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both an ordinary non-officer seaman and a classification or evaluation given to something.

clue.text: Physics unit in graduate's laboratory

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the following words, spanning the gap between them

blocks.note: runs across the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A unit of measurement used in a graduate student's lab.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is ignored when reading the run of letters across the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: The tesla is the SI unit of magnetic flux density, named after the inventor Nikola Tesla.

clue.text: A celebrant improvised a place of worship

indicators.note: improvised means made up on the spot, so the letters are put together freshly

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A priest leading a service made up a makeshift church.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition has its own 'a', so the clue begins and ends with one; the first belongs to the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A tabernacle is a house of worship, originally the portable sanctuary the Israelites carried through the wilderness.

clue.text: Observed No 5 dropping out

indicators.note: something dropping out leaves the group, so those letters are removed from the word

blocks.note: No is short for number, and the setter's number here is seven
the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: Someone spotted that the fifth item on a list has gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No 5' wants to be read together as 'number five'; split it: 'No' is any number, and only seven loses a V to leave a word meaning observed. A loose but fair hint for four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Seen is the past participle of see, which matches the passive sense of observed, meaning noticed or witnessed.

clue.text: Total set of books held in Ireland

indicators.note: something held in another is enclosed by it, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: the Irish-language name of the country
the New Testament, a collection of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A complete collection of books kept in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set of books' reads as a library; in crosswords it is usually the Old or New Testament, OT or NT.
explanation.definitionFit: Entire means whole or complete, with nothing left out, the adjectival sense of total here.

clue.text: Where cobbler would work finally

blocks.note: first meaning: at the foot-shaped block on which shoes are made or mended
second meaning: after a long wait

explanation.walkthrough: A last is the shoe-shaped form a cobbler, or shoe repairer, works on, so the cobbler sits at one.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an everyday expression for something happening eventually, after much delay, and literally places the shoemaker at his block.
